name: Acetyl tetrapeptide-2

card.summary: A thymopoietin-mimic cosmetic peptide with cell-culture data and one combination-lotion hair study.
card.note: No trial of the peptide alone; the hair study used a multi-ingredient lotion.

quick.overview:
Acetyl tetrapeptide-2 is a short cosmetic peptide marketed for firmness and skin regeneration, and also appears in some hair lotions.

Research is thin: a keratinocyte cell study and a randomized study of a lotion that combined it with creatine and B vitamins.
quick.mechanism: Suppliers say it mimics thymopoietin and prompts keratinocytes to release GM-CSF, activating skin Langerhans cells. In cultured cells it raised stiffness and COL17A1 expression.
quick.risks: No safety data were found beyond its status as a cosmetic ingredient; the supporting claims are largely manufacturer-reported.

lead: Acetyl tetrapeptide-2 is a synthetic four-amino-acid peptide (acetyl-Lys-Asp-Val-Tyr) used in skin-firming and anti-aging cosmetics and in some hair lotions, sold by suppliers under names such as Thymulen 4.[1] It is aimed at making skin look firmer and more youthful, and at supporting the look of fuller hair in lotions where it is combined with other actives.[1][3]

It is described as mimicking thymopoietin, a thymus hormone, and is claimed to counter the age-related decline of thymic factors and to support skin immune defences and epidermal regeneration.[1] A 2018 cell study found that the peptide changed the stiffness and gene expression of cultured keratinocytes.[2]

In a 2021 randomized controlled study of 100 women with acute telogen effluvium, a lotion combining the peptide with creatine and B vitamins was reported by the authors to appear to accelerate recovery from the condition, with higher anagen-to-telogen ratios at weeks 4 and 8 than the shampoo-only group.[3][4] No trial has tested the peptide alone on facial wrinkles or firmness.

chain: Peptide applied in a serum, cream or hair lotion
Keratinocyte activity and skin-cell signalling are affected in lab tests
Skin is marketed as firmer and hair loss as reduced during telogen effluvium
angle.text: The peptide is included in serums and creams marketed to make skin look firmer, and in a hair lotion that was tested in women with temporary shedding. The measured hair result comes from the combined lotion, not the peptide on its own.

paras: Supplier-derived descriptions say the peptide stimulates keratinocytes to produce GM-CSF, which promotes maturation of Langerhans cells and thereby raises skin immune surveillance.[1] Such descriptions are manufacturer claims and have not been independently tested in published trials.

A 2021 open, randomized controlled study (Turlier and colleagues) in 100 women aged 19 to 50 with acute telogen effluvium compared a lotion containing creatine, acetyl tetrapeptide-2 and B vitamins plus a mild shampoo (51 women) with the mild shampoo alone (49 women). Both groups had a higher anagen-to-telogen ratio at week 16 than at baseline. The lotion group showed significantly higher ratios at weeks 4 and 8, a significant fall in telogen hair density at all time points, and investigator-rated improvement in hair density, and the lotion was well tolerated.[3][4] Because the lotion combined several actives and the control was shampoo alone, the results cannot be attributed to the peptide by itself.
No studies were found of acetyl tetrapeptide-2 as a single ingredient in facial skin.

In immortalized human keratinocytes (HaCaT), atomic force microscopy showed that the peptide raised cell stiffness after 48 hours, most notably at a low concentration, and it increased expression of the COL17A1 gene.[2] This was an in vitro study, not a test on living skin.
The peptide is marketed in serums, creams and masks.[1] No looksmaxxing community discussion was identified.

timeline.event: A cell study reports effects of the peptide on keratinocyte stiffness and COL17A1 expression.[2]
Randomized study of a multi-ingredient lotion containing the peptide in women with acute telogen effluvium is published.[3]
